### Lost Property

The lost-property office at Central Station was below everything else: below the platforms, below the café that sold coffee in three degrees of disappointment, below even the pipes that knocked in winter. Ada had worked there for thirty-one years.

Most of what came in was ordinary. Umbrellas multiplied in wet weather. Gloves arrived without their partners. There were keys, library books, a surprising number of artificial teeth, and once a wedding cake, still wearing its little bride and groom.

But people lost other things too, things no cloakroom ticket could account for: a baritone voice, the smell of July, nine seconds of courage tied with string. These were kept on the upper shelves, labelled in Ada’s small, upright hand.

The office closed at midnight. At eleven fifty-three on a wet Thursday, a boy came in.

He was perhaps eleven, with rain on his eyelashes and one shoelace trailing. He stood just inside the door, as though the room might change its mind about admitting him.

“I’ve come to claim something,” he said.

Ada put down her pen. “Do you have a ticket?”

“No.”

“A date?”

He shook his head.

“Can you describe it?”

“My father’s laugh.”

Ada did not tell him he was in the wrong place. After thirty-one years, she knew better than to hurry people toward sensible explanations.

“What was it like?” she asked.

The boy considered.

“It started low,” he said. “Like an engine that wouldn’t. Then it got away from him. He’d try to keep talking, but he couldn’t, and that made it worse. My mum used to put down whatever she was holding when it happened. Even if it was a knife. Especially if it was a knife.”

Ada waited.

“He died in March,” the boy said. “I thought there’d be more of it left in the house.”

The pipes knocked above them. Somewhere far overhead, a train pulled away.

Ada rose and took the stepladder from its hook.

She found what she was looking for on the fourth shelf, behind a violin case containing only winter. It was a shallow cardboard box, the sort that had once held a shirt. Its label was yellowed, but the writing was still clear:

**ONE LAUGH. UNCLAIMED. HANDLE WITH CARE.**

“There’s a procedure,” Ada said. “You must listen all the way through. Then you decide whether it’s yours.”

The boy nodded.

She set the box on the counter and lifted the lid.

First came the small, unwilling engine sound. Then a snort. Then the laugh broke loose entirely: huge, helpless, magnificently undignified. It filled the low room and rattled the umbrella stand. Somewhere inside it were a summer garden, a badly told joke, a table set for too many people, and a man who had momentarily forgotten every reason not to be happy.

Ada laughed too. She could not help it.

The boy cried and smiled at the same time, which looked difficult but apparently wasn’t.

When the sound faded, he leaned toward the box.

“That’s it,” he whispered. “That’s exactly it.”

Ada closed the lid gently.

“Can I take it?” he asked.

She opened the ledger. There were rules about these things, columns for names and dates and signatures, rules designed by people who had never had to catalogue nine seconds of courage. Ada looked at the boy’s wet sleeves, at the shoelace he had finally noticed and was pressing beneath one shoe.

“It’s yours to look after,” she said.

He took the box in both arms.

“Will it run out?”

“Not if you use it,” Ada said, then wished she hadn’t. It sounded like something printed on a mug.

But the boy nodded, as if this were perfectly sensible.

At the door he stopped.

“Do people come back for most things?”

“No,” Ada said. “Mostly they buy new umbrellas.”

He thought about this. “That’s stupid.”

“Often.”

He went up the stairs, carefully, without looking back.

Ada sat for a while with the ledger open. Then, where she usually wrote **RETURNED TO OWNER**, she wrote **RETURNED TO USE**.

She switched off the lights. On the shelves above her, thousands of unclaimed things shifted and settled in the dark. For years that sound had seemed mournful to her, like a house remembering its absences.

That night, it sounded different.

It sounded impatient.
